newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finance ministers meet on post-EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Finance ministers meet on post-EMU budget pact.

text.p: European Union finance ministers met on Monday to try to agree a new system for ensuring that countries in a single currency maintain the required budgetary discipline after joining.
Negotiations on a budget stability pact have been deadlocked due to German demands for much more stringent rules.
Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, chairman of the meeting, said he expected the ministers to advance their plans, but was not sure whether an agreement could be reached.
"We'll make some progress but how far we get remains to be seen. All the indications are very positive," Quinn said as he arrived for the meeting.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto also said chances of reaching an agreement were more positive than advertised.
"The situation is better than expected," he said.
The effort to secure a budget stability pact has become one of the most difficult hurdles in nailing down a blueprint for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Under a proposed plan, countries running annual deficits above three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) could face stiff fines if they failed to curb expenditure.
But if a government could show that a severe recession was behind the deterioration of its public finances, it might be able to avoid sanctions.

Germany wants the recession defined as a two percent annual decline in GDP. Others have argued for a less rigid approach, preferring a range -- a fall in output of between 0.5 and 2.0 percent -- that would force EU finance ministers to decide whether fines were appropriate.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on Monday said the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit should be made after a proper evaluation of a country's economic circumstances.
"France's position is simple and clear. It is up to the (finance ministers) to decide on a case by case basis," Arthuis said in a newspaper interview.
Taking a shot at Germany's intransigent bargaining stance, Arthuis added: "When you're in a community you have to try to reach a consensus rather than imposing your point of view."
The inflexible posture of Germany was noted by others as well.

Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, told reporters that the differences among the 15 EU nations over the budget pact were mostly of "emphasis," with Britain more open than some its partners.
"We are more flexible I think than the Germans might be inclined to be," Clarke said.
He added that Britain would reserve judgement on any political decision taken on Monday.

If finance ministers do not agree on Monday, it is likely that EU leaders meeting at a summit in Dublin on December 13 will be able to agree only an outline of a plan, leaving a firm decision until the next summit, in June.
Separately, the ministers are likely to agree a blueprint for a new Exchange Rate Mechanism that will link the single currency to those not participating among the first wave of countries in 1999.
They are also expected to bring forward legislation that establishes a legal framework for monetary union.
